title: Overview
content:
Overview In this workshop, we build a solution for automated infrastructure deployment and network monitoring on AWS.
Terraform provisions the infrastructure, deploys an Amazon EC2 web server, and configures monitoring components. VPC Flow Logs collect network traffic information, Amazon CloudWatch analyzes it, and Amazon SNS delivers alarm notifications.
1. Business Scenario A technical team operating a web application on AWS needs to:
Deploy infrastructure with consistent configuration. Control connections to the server. Observe accepted and rejected network traffic. Find information to troubleshoot connectivity issues. Receive notifications when traffic matches a configured alert condition. Manually configuring multiple resources can introduce errors and make environments difficult to reproduce. Without logs and alerts, administrators may also struggle to identify why connections fail.
This workshop addresses these challenges by combining Infrastructure as Code with AWS monitoring services.
2. System Architecture The solution is deployed in ap-southeast-1 (Singapore).
The main components are:
A VPC containing a public subnet and a private subnet. An Internet Gateway and a route table for the public subnet. An Ubuntu EC2 instance running Nginx in the public subnet. A Security Group restricting inbound server connections. VPC Flow Logs publishing traffic information to CloudWatch Logs. A metric filter and CloudWatch Alarm tracking rejected records. Amazon SNS delivering notifications to a confirmed email address. A CloudWatch Dashboard displaying monitoring metrics. The private subnet demonstrates network segmentation. It contains no instances and has no Internet route.
Architecture Diagram !(/images/1/ntd1.png)
3. AWS Services and Tools Service / Tool Role Reason for Selection Amazon VPC Organize the network, subnets, and routing Provides control over network structure and connectivity Amazon EC2 Run Ubuntu and the Nginx web server Provides a simple environment for connectivity testing AWS IAM Grant permissions to users and services Supports roles and scoped access VPC Flow Logs Collect network flow information Helps analyze accepted and rejected connections Amazon CloudWatch Store logs, run queries, display metrics, and evaluate alarms Centralizes monitoring capabilities Amazon SNS Deliver email notifications Integrates easily with CloudWatch alarms Terraform Provision and manage infrastructure as code Enables repeatable deployment using consistent configuration 4. Network Design Component Planned Configuration Region ap-southeast-1 VPC CIDR 10.10.0.0/16 Public subnet 10.10.1.0/24 Private subnet 10.10.2.0/24 Server Ubuntu 24.04 LTS on EC2 Web service Nginx, TCP/80 Allowed web source The participant’s public IPv4 address with a /32 suffix Blocked connection test port TCP/8080 Public subnet Internet route Internet Gateway Private subnet Internet route Not configured The Security Group allows TCP/80 only from the configured source IP. TCP/8080 remains closed for the rejected-traffic test.
5. Operational Workflow 5.1. Automated Deployment The participant writes Terraform configuration in VS Code. Terraform uses the configured AWS authentication credentials. Terraform creates networking, compute, and monitoring resources. EC2 runs user data to install and start Nginx automatically. 5.2. Allowed Access The participant accesses the EC2 public IP using HTTP. Traffic reaches the server through the Internet Gateway. The Security Group allows TCP/80 from the configured source IP. Nginx returns the web page. VPC Flow Logs record information about the accepted traffic. 5.3. Rejected Connection Detection The participant attempts a TCP/8080 connection to EC2. The Security Group has no rule allowing this connection. If the traffic reaches the EC2 network interface and is logged, Flow Logs produce a record with the REJECT action. The record is delivered to CloudWatch Logs. A metric filter counts REJECT records for TCP/8080 directed to the server’s private IP. A CloudWatch alarm evaluates the configured metric threshold. When the alarm transitions to ALARM, SNS sends an email. 5.4. System Observation The administrator uses a CloudWatch Dashboard to view incoming traffic, outgoing traffic, and rejected records matching the metric filter.
Logs Insights is used to search and summarize records within a selected time range.
6. Security and Cost Considerations Use an account or role authorized for the workshop. Avoid using the root user for deployment. Do not embed access keys or secret keys in source code. Scope IAM permissions to the required actions and resources. Restrict web access to the participant’s public IP. Limit log retention to control stored data volume. Do not deploy a NAT Gateway for this lab. Remove resources after collecting the required evidence. 7. Results to Demonstrate Validation Item Expected Result Infrastructure deployment Terraform creates the resources successfully Web access The Nginx page loads from the allowed source IP Blocked-port test A matching TCP/8080 REJECT record is available Monitoring The dashboard displays data Alerting The alarm transitions to ALARM and an email is sent Cleanup Workshop resources are removed 8. Scope and Limitations The solution uses one EC2 instance and is not highly available. No application is deployed in the private subnet. Flow Logs capture metadata, not packet payloads. Log delivery is delayed rather than real-time packet monitoring. A flow record can aggregate multiple packets. A REJECT record does not automatically indicate an attack. The solution sends alerts but does not automatically remediate incidents. Detailed deployment and validation instructions are provided in the following sections.

In-Depth Study of Amazon EC2 and Associated Storage Mechanisms Weekly Objectives Master the architecture, lifecycle, and pricing models of Amazon EC2. Practice automating and deploying virtual servers (Instances) in the cloud environment. Configure virtual firewalls (Security Groups) and manage access keys (Key Pairs) securely. Deep dive into AWS Block Storage types, especially Amazon EBS and backup mechanisms (Snapshots). Differentiate storage types: EBS, Instance Store, and Amazon EFS. Tasks Performed 1. Deploy and Manage Amazon EC2 Initialize virtual servers: Practiced creating EC2 instances running Amazon Linux 2023 and Ubuntu 22.04. Learned how to select appropriate Amazon Machine Images (AMI). Select Instance Type: Researched the differences between instance families (General Purpose - T3/M5, Compute Optimized - C5, Memory Optimized - R5) and experimented with the t2.micro type (Free Tier eligible). Connection Methods: Practiced connecting to Linux servers via SSH using Terminal (Mac/Linux) and PuTTY (Windows) with .pem / .ppk key files. Experienced the EC2 Instance Connect feature for direct browser access without managing physical Key Pairs. User Data: Wrote simple Bash scripts in the User Data section during EC2 initialization to automatically install a web server (Apache/Nginx) and display a “Hello World” HTML page upon boot. 2. Configure Security Groups Analyzed the working principles of Security Groups (Stateful firewall) vs. Network ACLs (Stateless firewall). Configured Inbound Rules to allow traffic: Opened port 22 (SSH) restricted to personal Public IP for security. Opened ports 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS) to allow global access to the web server (0.0.0.0/0). 3. Configure and Manage Amazon EBS (Elastic Block Store) Initialize and Attach Volumes: Created independent EBS Volumes, selected gp3 (General Purpose SSD) for cost/performance optimization, and attached them to running EC2 instances. Format and Mount Volumes on Linux: Used the lsblk command to check attached devices. Formatted the new volume using the sudo mkfs -t xfs /dev/xvdf command. Created a directory and mounted the volume to the Linux file system (sudo mount /dev/xvdf /data), then configured the /etc/fstab file to ensure the volume automounts upon reboot. Data Backup (EBS Snapshots): Practiced creating Snapshots to backup EBS volume data. Then, tested deleting the current volume, creating a new Volume from the saved Snapshot, and reattaching it to the EC2 instance to verify data recovery capabilities. 4. Explore EC2 Pricing Models Read documentation and compared models: On-Demand (pay-as-you-go, most flexible), Reserved Instances (1-3 year commitment, high savings), Savings Plans, and Spot Instances (utilizing spare capacity at extremely low costs but can be interrupted at any time). Achievements Successfully deployed a basic web server on EC2 accessible via the Internet. Gained a deep understanding of how the OS interacts with EBS virtual drives and how to manipulate partitions on Linux. Learned how to optimize costs when selecting EC2 types and EBS Volumes based on project needs. Challenges and Solutions Challenge 1: When initially creating an EC2 instance, could not SSH into the server and encountered a Connection Timed Out error. Solution: Checked the Security Group and realized Port 22 was not open for the personal IP. After adding the rule, the connection was successful. Challenge 2: When attaching a new EBS volume, copied files into the mount directory, but after rebooting the EC2 instance, the data in that directory disappeared (volume did not automount). Solution: Researched AWS documentation and Linux OS, realized the need to configure the /etc/fstab file with the volume’s UUID to automate mounting upon boot.

Comprehensive Infrastructure as Code (IaC) and Observability Solution 1. Executive Summary This project focuses on solving the challenges of cloud network administration and operations by fully automating the infrastructure provisioning process and establishing a real-time network traffic monitoring mechanism. The solution aims to eliminate error-prone manual configurations (Click-Ops) while providing the capability to quickly detect, alert, and remediate connectivity issues or security vulnerabilities.
Within the scope of this internship report, the network system is built and managed according to enterprise standards on the AWS platform:
Automation: Utilizing AWS CloudFormation to declare the entire network topology (VPC, Subnets, Route Tables, NAT Gateway) as code (IaC), combined with a CI/CD pipeline via AWS CodePipeline/CodeBuild for consistent deployment. Monitoring & Analysis: Integrating VPC Flow Logs to push data to Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights for detailed access flow analysis (ACCEPT/REJECT). Additionally, applying advanced diagnostic tools like AWS Reachability Analyzer and Network Access Analyzer to mathematically verify network paths and firewall integrity (Security Groups & NACLs). 2. Problem Statement Current Issues
Operating network infrastructure via manual methods (Click-Ops) frequently leads to human errors, causing configuration drift to accumulate and making it difficult to trace changes[cite: 5]. As the system scales, the lack of visibility into internal traffic (east-west traffic) and the inability to automatically detect and alert on anomalous access expose the system to significant security risks and prolonged downtime[cite: 5].
Solution
The project centralizes the entire network infrastructure lifecycle through Infrastructure as Code (IaC) combined with a CI/CD pipeline[cite: 5]. All network changes are version-controlled via Git and automatically deployed using AWS CloudFormation[cite: 5]. Simultaneously, the system deeply integrates VPC Flow Logs, analyzed via CloudWatch Logs Insights, and uses AWS Reachability Analyzer to proactively monitor and verify network paths in real-time[cite: 5].
Benefits and Return on Investment (ROI)
Eliminates 90% of manual infrastructure configuration time and standardizes Dev/Staging/Prod environments[cite: 5]. Maintains architectural integrity by instantly detecting network configuration deviations (Stack Drift)[cite: 5]. Comprehensive data flow observability, allowing alerts for network attacks (like port scanning) within minutes[cite: 5]. Optimizes costs by automatically cleaning up unused network resources via IaC[cite: 5]. 3. Solution Architecture AWS Services Used[cite: 7]
Category Service Role Network Amazon VPC, Internet/NAT Gateway, Route 53 Provides virtual private network, routing, and secure domain resolution[cite: 7]. Automation (IaC) AWS CloudFormation Declares and provisions all infrastructure resources as code (YAML)[cite: 7]. CI/CD Pipeline AWS CodePipeline, AWS CodeBuild Automated syntax testing (linting) and infrastructure deployment from Git[cite: 7]. Observability VPC Flow Logs, CloudWatch (Logs/Metrics/Alarms) Records network flow metadata, creates dashboards, and sets alert thresholds[cite: 7]. Security & Analysis Network Access Analyzer, Reachability Analyzer Mathematically verifies network paths, ensuring no unauthorized access[cite: 7]. Notifications Amazon SNS Sends immediate email/SMS alerts to administrators during network incidents[cite: 7]. Component Design[cite: 7]
IaC Repository: Network source code is stored in a Git repository. Any changes to Subnets or Security Groups require a Pull Request and review. Deployment Pipeline (network-pipeline 📄): Connects directly to Git. When the code is valid, CodeBuild triggers CloudFormation to update the infrastructure without causing downtime. Monitoring Engine: VPC Flow Logs collect network traffic metadata and push it to CloudWatch. Metric Filters will filter continuous REJECT actions to trigger SNS Alarms warning of Port Scanning risks. 4. Technical Implementation Deployment Phases[cite: 8]
Design & Analysis (Weeks 1–3): Review the current manual network structure, design a standard Multi-AZ architecture, and draw the network-architecture.drawio diagram 📄. IaC Development (Weeks 4–7): Write CloudFormation templates (infra/vpc-core.yaml 📄, infra/security.yaml 📄) to define Subnets, Route Tables, Security Groups[cite: 8]. CI/CD Automation (Weeks 8–9): Set up AWS CodePipeline connected to Git, integrating the cfn-lint tool to automatically check for syntax errors before deployment[cite: 8]. Monitoring & Optimization (Weeks 10–12): Enable VPC Flow Logs, build monitoring Dashboards on CloudWatch, configure CloudWatch Alarms, and run simulated disconnection tests to verify error catching capabilities[cite: 8]. Technical Requirements[cite: 8]
Local: Development environment with Git, AWS CLI, and the cfn-lint tool installed 📄[cite: 8]. AWS: Account with IAM admin privileges to create IAM Roles for the Pipeline, and permissions to operate VPC, CloudFormation, CodePipeline, and CloudWatch[cite: 8]. Third-party: GitHub/GitLab account to serve as the infrastructure source code repository[cite: 8]. 5. Roadmap & Milestones Phase Timeframe Key Milestone Architecture Analysis Weeks 1–3 Accurate network architecture diagram, CIDR analysis[cite: 8]. IaC Conversion Weeks 4–7 Completed CloudFormation template suite for Core VPC[cite: 8]. CI/CD Construction Weeks 8–9 Pipeline runs successfully, auto-deploys on new commits[cite: 8]. Monitoring Operations Weeks 10–12 CloudWatch dashboard active, SNS alerts triggered[cite: 8]. 6. Cost Estimation Operational costs are primarily focused on always-on services and log storage. Below is the estimation (can be further optimized via Free Tier):
NAT Gateway: ~$32/month (The most expensive component in the network architecture). VPC Flow Logs & CloudWatch: Depending on stored data volume (GB), estimated ~$5-10/month. CodePipeline/CodeBuild: Within the Free Tier limits for personal/learning projects. Total: ~$40-45/month for a standard lab environment. Or download the detailed budget estimate file from the AWS Pricing Calculator[cite: 9]. 7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix[cite: 9]
Risk Impact Probability IaC syntax error breaking active network connections High Medium[cite: 9] CloudFormation Stack Drift due to manual edits Medium High[cite: 9] CloudWatch Logs cost spike due to high log volume Medium Medium[cite: 9] False Positives from SNS rules Low High[cite: 9] Mitigation Strategies[cite: 9]
Always run automated testing (linting & validation) in CodePipeline before applying changes to the live environment[cite: 9]. Assign IAM Policies to lock down manual VPC edits on the Console, enforcing all configurations through IaC[cite: 9]. Set a Retention Period for CloudWatch Logs to 7-14 days to reduce storage costs[cite: 9]. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements[cite: 10]
Closed-loop management workflow: Push code -> CI/CD auto-checks -> Zero-downtime infrastructure deployment[cite: 10]. Centralized governance: The entire network topology is documented as code, making it easy to audit and rollback when necessary[cite: 10]. Real-time observability: Proactively monitor unauthorized access events instead of reacting passively[cite: 10]. Long-term Value[cite: 10]
Build a solid standard foundation (Network Landing Zone) for any future projects deployed on AWS[cite: 10]. Fully master the Cloud Network Operations (Cloud NetOps) mindset, a crucial skill for Systems / DevOps Engineers[cite: 10]. Easily scale out infrastructure to other Regions simply by changing environment variables in the code[cite: 10].

title: 5.2. Preparation
content:
5.2. Preparation Introduction Before deploying the Network Automation and Monitoring system on Amazon Web Services (AWS), we need to prepare the necessary environment, configure our AWS account, and become familiar with the AWS services used throughout this workshop.
Proper preparation helps ensure that the deployment process runs smoothly, reduces configuration errors, and provides a consistent environment for network monitoring and automation.
In this workshop, we will use the AWS Management Console to configure and manage AWS resources. The main services include Amazon VPC, Amazon EC2, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), Amazon CloudWatch, VPC Flow Logs, and Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS).
Objectives After completing this section, you will be able to:
Access and navigate the AWS Management Console. Select the appropriate AWS Region. Understand the main AWS services used in this workshop. Check IAM permissions and security settings. Prepare the environment for VPC and EC2 deployment. Access Amazon CloudWatch and Amazon SNS. Configure AWS Budgets to monitor estimated costs. 5.2.1. Prepare an AWS Account Step 1: Access the AWS Website First, open your web browser and visit the official AWS website:
AWS Website: https://aws.amazon.com/
If you do not have an AWS account, click Create an AWS Account to begin the registration process.
If you already have an account, select Sign In to the Console.
Figure 5.2.1. AWS official website.
Step 2: Create an AWS Account To create an AWS account, follow these steps:
Click Create an AWS Account. Enter your email address. Provide a name for your AWS account. Complete the account verification process. Enter the required contact information. Provide a valid payment method if requested. Complete identity verification. Select an available support plan and finish registration. AWS offers free usage allowances or credits for eligible accounts. However, not all AWS services are free, and usage beyond applicable limits may incur charges.
Figure 5.2.2. AWS account registration interface.
Step 3: Sign In to AWS Management Console After successfully creating your account:
Open https://console.aws.amazon.com/. Select the appropriate sign-in method. Enter your account credentials. Complete multi-factor authentication if required. Access the AWS Management Console. The AWS Management Console provides a centralized interface for managing cloud resources, monitoring services, and configuring AWS infrastructure.
Figure 5.2.3. AWS Management Console after signing in.
5.2.2. Select the AWS Region Step 1: Understand AWS Regions An AWS Region is a geographical area where AWS operates cloud infrastructure.
Each Region consists of multiple Availability Zones (AZs), which help improve application availability and fault tolerance.
For this workshop, we will use the following Region:
Configuration Value Region Name Asia Pacific (Singapore) Region Code ap-southeast-1 Deployment Platform AWS Management Console Using the same Region throughout the workshop helps simplify resource management and ensures that regional services can interact correctly.
Step 2: Change the AWS Region Follow these steps:
Sign in to the AWS Management Console. Locate the Region selector in the upper-right corner. Click the currently selected Region. Find Asia Pacific (Singapore). Select Asia Pacific (Singapore). Verify that the Region is set to ap-southeast-1. Figure 5.2.4. Selecting the Asia Pacific (Singapore) Region.
Note: Regional resources such as VPC, EC2, CloudWatch, and SNS should be configured in the selected Region. IAM is a global AWS service.
5.2.3. Understand the AWS Services Before deploying the system, we need to understand the primary services used in the network automation and monitoring architecture.
AWS Service Purpose Amazon VPC Creates an isolated virtual network Amazon EC2 Provides virtual servers for testing AWS IAM Manages identities and permissions VPC Flow Logs Captures network traffic metadata Amazon CloudWatch Collects and analyzes logs and metrics Amazon SNS Sends monitoring notifications AWS Systems Manager Helps manage and access EC2 instances Elastic Load Balancing Distributes incoming application traffic EC2 Auto Scaling Automatically adjusts EC2 capacity These services work together to provide a cloud environment capable of collecting network logs, monitoring network activity, detecting specified events, and sending alerts.
The detailed configuration of these services will be introduced in the following sections.
5.2.4. Check AWS IAM Permissions AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is a service that allows administrators to securely control access to AWS resources.
IAM helps determine which users, roles, and services are allowed to perform specific actions.
Step 1: Open the IAM Console Go to the AWS Management Console. Locate the search bar at the top of the page. Type IAM. Select IAM from the search results. Wait for the IAM Dashboard to appear. Figure 5.2.5. AWS IAM Dashboard.
Step 2: Check IAM Access In the IAM Console, review the following sections:
Users: Manage IAM users. User groups: Organize users into groups. Roles: Define permissions that AWS services or identities can assume. Policies: Define allowed and denied actions. For this workshop, the working identity needs appropriate permissions to manage:
Amazon VPC and network resources. Amazon EC2 instances. IAM roles and policies required by the workshop. Amazon CloudWatch Logs and Alarms. VPC Flow Logs. Amazon SNS topics and subscriptions. AWS Systems Manager resources. Use the principle of least privilege, granting only the permissions necessary to complete the workshop.
Avoid using the AWS root user for daily operations. Enable multi-factor authentication (MFA) to improve account security.
Figure 5.2.6. Checking IAM access and permissions.
Note: You do not need to create new IAM roles at this stage. Required service roles will be configured during the deployment and monitoring sections.
5.2.5. Prepare the Amazon VPC Environment Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) enables users to create an isolated virtual network within AWS.
In this workshop, Amazon VPC will provide the network infrastructure for the EC2 instance and monitoring services.
Step 1: Open the VPC Console Return to the AWS Management Console. Enter VPC in the search bar. Select the VPC service. Locate Your VPCs in the left navigation menu. Click Your VPCs. The console displays the VPCs currently available in the selected Region.
Figure 5.2.7. Amazon VPC management interface.
Step 2: Explore VPC Components In the left navigation menu, locate the following components:
1. Your VPCs
Displays existing virtual private networks.
2. Subnets
Allows users to divide a VPC into smaller network segments.
3. Route Tables
Defines how network traffic is routed between subnets and other destinations.
4. Internet Gateways
Provides a connection between a VPC and the Internet when routing and access settings permit it.
5. Security Groups
Controls allowed inbound and outbound traffic for associated resources.
6. Flow Logs
Captures metadata about network traffic passing through network interfaces.
At this stage, we only need to become familiar with these components.
The actual VPC, subnet, route table, and security group configuration will be performed in Section 5.3: Network and EC2 Deployment.
5.2.6. Prepare the Amazon EC2 Environment Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) provides scalable virtual computing resources in the AWS Cloud.
In this workshop, an EC2 instance will serve as a test server for network connectivity and traffic monitoring.
Step 1: Open the EC2 Console Return to the AWS Management Console. Search for EC2. Select the EC2 service. In the left navigation menu, click Instances. Review the list of existing instances. Figure 5.2.8. Amazon EC2 Instances interface.
Step 2: Check the EC2 Deployment Environment Before launching an instance, check the following information:
The selected AWS Region. Available EC2 instance types. Available Amazon Machine Images (AMIs). Instance quotas and account eligibility. Permissions to launch EC2 instances. AWS Systems Manager access requirements. For this workshop, we plan to use an Amazon Linux instance to generate test traffic and verify network monitoring.
The instance type will be selected based on the available resources and cost considerations.
Important: Do not launch an EC2 instance yet. The virtual network must be configured first.
The EC2 instance will be created in Section 5.3.
5.2.7. Prepare Amazon CloudWatch Amazon CloudWatch is a monitoring and observability service that provides information about AWS resources, applications, and system performance.
In this workshop, CloudWatch will be responsible for collecting, analyzing, and displaying network monitoring information.
Step 1: Open Amazon CloudWatch Sign in to the AWS Management Console. Search for CloudWatch. Select CloudWatch. Wait for the CloudWatch console to load. Explore the navigation menu. Figure 5.2.9. Amazon CloudWatch overview.
Step 2: Explore Monitoring Features The following features will be used throughout the workshop:
CloudWatch Logs
Stores and manages log data collected from AWS resources.
CloudWatch Metrics
Provides numerical measurements used to monitor system performance and events.
CloudWatch Alarms
Monitors metrics and changes alarm states when predefined conditions are met.
CloudWatch Dashboards
Displays monitoring information in a centralized visual interface.
During deployment, VPC Flow Logs will be configured to send traffic metadata to CloudWatch Logs.
We will then create metric filters and alarms to detect rejected network traffic.
For example, the workshop will monitor rejected TCP traffic on port 8080.
A metric filter can identify matching log events, while CloudWatch Alarms can monitor the resulting metric.
Note: No log groups or alarms need to be created in this preparation section.
These configurations will be covered in Section 5.4: Monitoring Configuration.
5.2.8. Prepare Amazon SNS Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) is a managed messaging service that enables notifications to be sent to subscribed endpoints.
In this workshop, Amazon SNS will be integrated with CloudWatch Alarms to deliver email notifications when monitoring conditions are triggered.
Step 1: Open the Amazon SNS Console Return to the AWS Management Console. Search for SNS. Select Simple Notification Service. Open the SNS console. Locate Topics and Subscriptions in the navigation menu. Figure 5.2.10. Amazon SNS management interface.
Step 2: Understand SNS Components SNS Topic
A communication channel used to publish messages to subscribers.
SNS Subscription
Connects a subscriber, such as an email address, to an SNS topic.
When the monitoring system detects an event that causes a CloudWatch Alarm to change state, the alarm can publish a notification to an SNS topic.
Amazon SNS then sends the notification to confirmed subscribers.
For this workshop, email will be used as the notification method.
The SNS topic and email subscription will be configured in the monitoring workflow.
5.2.9. Configure AWS Budgets Monitoring AWS costs is an important part of working with cloud infrastructure.
Some AWS resources, including EC2 instances, CloudWatch Logs, load balancers, and network services, may generate charges depending on usage and account eligibility.
AWS Budgets allows users to define spending thresholds and receive notifications when costs approach or exceed those thresholds.
Step 1: Open AWS Billing Go to the AWS Management Console. Search for Billing and Cost Management. Open the Billing console. Locate Budgets in the navigation menu. Click Budgets. Step 2: Create a Cost Budget Click Create budget. Choose Cost budget or an appropriate cost-budget template. Select Monthly as the budget period. Enter a budget amount based on your requirements. Configure notification thresholds. Enter an email address for alerts. Review the budget configuration. Click Create budget. For example, you can set a monthly budget of 5 USD as an initial monitoring threshold.
This amount is only an example and does not guarantee that the workshop will cost less than 5 USD.
Figure 5.2.11. Configuring AWS Budgets for cost monitoring.
Important: AWS Budgets does not automatically stop all running resources when a spending threshold is reached. Cost reporting and notifications may also be delayed.
Always review resource pricing and delete unused resources after completing the workshop.
5.2.10. Verify the Preparation Environment After completing the previous steps, verify that the AWS environment is ready for deployment.
No. Component Expected Result 1 AWS Account Successfully signed in 2 AWS Region ap-southeast-1 3 AWS IAM Appropriate permissions available 4 Amazon VPC Console accessible 5 Amazon EC2 Instance management accessible 6 Amazon CloudWatch Monitoring console accessible 7 Amazon SNS SNS console accessible 8 AWS Budgets Cost monitoring configured Expected Results After completing this preparation section, you should have:
Successfully accessed the AWS Management Console. Selected the Asia Pacific (Singapore) Region. Understood the main AWS services used in the workshop. Checked the necessary IAM permissions. Explored the VPC and EC2 management interfaces. Accessed CloudWatch and SNS. Configured cost monitoring through AWS Budgets. Prepared the AWS environment for network deployment. Conclusion In this section, we completed the preparation steps required to build a network automation and monitoring system on AWS.
We became familiar with the AWS Management Console, selected the deployment Region, reviewed the essential services, and checked the permissions and cost monitoring settings.
These preparations provide the foundation for deploying a virtual network and configuring monitoring capabilities in the following sections.
In the next section, 5.3. Network and EC2 Deployment, we will create and configure the core network infrastructure, including:
Amazon VPC Public Subnet Internet Gateway Route Table Security Group Amazon EC2 Instance After deploying these resources, we will test network connectivity and prepare the infrastructure for VPC Flow Logs and CloudWatch monitoring.

title: Network and EC2 Deployment
content:
1. Objectives This section explains how to create the network infrastructure and configure an EC2 instance to install Nginx automatically through user data.
The tasks include:
Create a VPC, a public subnet, and a private subnet. Verify route tables and the internet gateway. Create a security group that allows HTTP access from the workshop client’s IP address. Configure EC2 and enable EBS volume encryption. Enter user data to install Nginx automatically. Launch EC2 and record the information required for monitoring. The deployment shown in the screenshots uses United States (N. Virginia) — us-east-1. The EC2 configuration screenshot shows a Canonical Ubuntu 26.04 AMI.
Region consistency: If you continue with the deployment shown in these screenshots, update the Region in sections 5.1, 5.2, and the monitoring configuration in section 5.4 to us-east-1. The aws:RequestedRegion conditions and ARNs containing a Region in the permissions policies must also be updated accordingly. Editing Markdown does not change AWS resources or permissions.
2. Information Displayed value IPv4 CIDR 10.10.1.0/24 State Available Availability Zone us-east-1a VPC aws-network-workshop-vpc Route table aws-network-workshop-rtb-public Auto-assign public IPv4 address No Record the VPC ID and Public subnet ID for the EC2 configuration.

6. Create the Security Group 6.1. Enter the Security Group Details Open EC2 → Security Groups. Choose Create security group. Enter: Field Value Security group name aws-network-workshop-web-sg Description HTTP access from workshop client VPC The workshop VPC 6.2. Configure the Inbound Rule Under Inbound rules, choose Add rule and set Type → HTTP.
In the screenshot:
Type is set to HTTP. Protocol is TCP. Port range is 80. Source type is still Custom. The Source field is empty. Complete the source configuration:
Click an empty area to close the suggestions currently open in the Source field. Open the Source type dropdown, which currently displays Custom. Select My IP. Confirm that AWS fills in the workshop client’s public IP address in the format x.x.x.x/32. Save the following inbound rule:
Type Protocol Port range Source HTTP TCP 80 The workshop client’s public IP address /32 Leave port 8080 absent from the inbound allow rules for the later REJECT test. This lab does not require an SSH rule on port 22.

Configure: Setting Value Name aws-network-workshop-web AMI shown in the workshop screenshot Canonical Ubuntu 26.04 Architecture amd64 / x86_64 Instance type t3.micro Key pair Proceed without a key pair Number of instances 1 The Number of instances field is located in the Summary panel on the right side of the launch page.

Confirm that the final configuration displays Encrypted. Screenshot 3 records the volume before encryption was enabled. 8. Install Nginx Automatically with User Data 8.1. Open Advanced Details Scroll down and expand Advanced details.
Configure:
Setting Value IAM instance profile Leave empty Detailed CloudWatch monitoring Keep disabled; use basic monitoring Metadata version V2 only / token required, if shown The workshop-flowlogs-role role is configured for the flow log in section 5.4.

Updates package lists. Installs Nginx. Creates an HTML page for testing. Enables and starts the Nginx service. Leave User data has already been base64 encoded unchecked.
Enter user data before launching the instance. Verify the installation and website access in section 5.5.
9. Launch and Inspect EC2 9.1. Review Before Launch Confirm that:
Number of instances is 1. The correct AMI and t3.micro instance type are selected. EC2 is in the public subnet. Auto-assign public IP is enabled. The correct security group is selected. The root volume is 8 GiB and uses gp3. Root volume encryption is enabled. The complete user data script has been entered. Choose Launch instance.
9.2. Inspect After Launch Choose View all instances. Open aws-network-workshop-web. Wait for the Running state and successful status checks. Under Details, verify the VPC, subnet, public IPv4, and private IPv4 addresses. Under Security, verify the security group and saved rules. Under Storage, record the root volume ID and inspect the volume’s encryption information. Record the actual values:
Information Actual value Region us-east-1 VPC ID Record from the AWS console Public subnet ID Record from the AWS console Instance ID Record after launch EC2 public IPv4 Record after launch EC2 private IPv4 Record after launch Workshop client’s public IP Record from the saved My IP rule Root EBS volume ID Record from the Storage tab The Running state does not establish that Nginx is successfully serving HTTP. Test the website in section 5.5.
10. Review the Evidence 10.1. Completion Checklist Mark each item only after verifying the actual result in AWS:
The VPC and both subnets use the correct CIDR blocks. The public route table has a default route to the internet gateway. The private subnet uses the correct route table. The saved HTTP 80 rule uses the workshop client’s IP address with /32. Port 8080 remains absent from inbound allow rules. Root volume encryption and Delete on termination are enabled. Worklog Week 3: Setting Up Advanced Object Storage with Amazon S3 Weekly Objectives Understand the core concepts of Amazon S3, including buckets, objects, and global namespaces. Host a static website using S3 and configure public access securely. Implement data protection mechanisms such as S3 Versioning and Server-Side Encryption (SSE). Explore S3 Storage Classes and automate cost optimization using Lifecycle Policies. Practice interacting with S3 via the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI). Tasks Performed 1. Bucket Creation and Object Management Basic Operations: Created S3 buckets in different AWS Regions. Uploaded, downloaded, and organized files using the AWS Management Console. AWS CLI Integration: Configured the AWS CLI with IAM credentials. Practiced executing CLI commands (aws s3 mb, aws s3 cp, aws s3 sync, aws s3 ls) to automate bulk file uploads and synchronization between local directories and S3 buckets. 2. Static Website Hosting Configuration: Enabled the “Static website hosting” feature on a dedicated bucket. Uploaded index.html and error.html files. Access Management: Navigated the “Block Public Access” settings. Authored and attached a custom JSON Bucket Policy to grant s3:GetObject permissions to the public, successfully making the website accessible via the S3 endpoint URL. 3. Data Security and Protection S3 Versioning: Enabled Versioning on a critical data bucket. Tested uploading multiple files with the same name and observed how S3 assigns unique version IDs, allowing for the restoration of previous file states. Encryption: Configured default Server-Side Encryption using Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3) to ensure all newly uploaded objects are automatically encrypted at rest. 4. Storage Classes and Lifecycle Rules Storage Class Analysis: Researched the performance and pricing differences between S3 Standard, S3 Standard-IA (Infrequent Access), and Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. Lifecycle Automation: Created a Lifecycle Rule to automatically transition objects that have not been accessed for 30 days to the S3 Standard-IA storage class, and move them to S3 Glacier after 90 days to optimize storage costs. Achievements Successfully deployed and hosted a fully functional static website on Amazon S3 without needing a traditional web server. Gained proficiency in using AWS CLI for faster and scriptable storage management. Implemented best practices for data retention, backup, and cost management using S3 features. Challenges and Solutions Challenge 1: Encountered a 403 Forbidden error when trying to access the static website via the provided endpoint. Solution: Realized that AWS enables “Block all public access” by default for new buckets. I had to explicitly disable this feature and then verify that the JSON syntax in my Bucket Policy correctly specified the bucket ARN with /* at the end to grant access to all objects inside it. Challenge 2: Confused about how to permanently delete an object when Versioning is enabled. Solution: Learned that a standard delete action only inserts a “Delete Marker”. To permanently delete the file, I had to toggle the “Show versions” option in the console and delete the specific version ID, or use the --version-id flag in the AWS CLI.

Creating an Admin Group Log in to the Control Panel on the AWS Web Service page.
Click on your account name at the top right corner and select My Security Credentials.
Note: If you don’t see the My Security Credentials menu, you can click on the search icon and type IAM. Then click on the IAM service to access the IAM management interface.
On the left sidebar, choose User Groups, and then select Create Group.
Under the Name the group section, enter the Group name (For example: AdminGroup), and scroll down.
In the Attach permissions policies section, type AdministratorAccess in the search bar and select it. Finally, click on Create Group.
The creation of the admin group is complete.
Create Admin User You can use the AWS Management Console to create IAM users.
Follow the sign-in procedure appropriate to your user type as described in the topic How to sign in to AWS in the AWS Sign-In User Guide.
On the Console Home page, select the IAM service.
In the navigation pane, select Users, and then select Add users.
On the Specify user details page, under User details, enter the new user’s name in the User name field. This will be their sign-in name for AWS.
Note: User names can be up to 64 letters, digits, and certain characters: plus (+), equal (=), comma (,), period (.), at sign (@), underscore (_), and hyphen (-). User names must be unique within an account, and they are case-sensitive when used in policies or ARNs. However, they are case-insensitive during the sign-in process.
Select Provide user access to the AWS Management Console. This generates AWS Management Console sign-in credentials for the new user.
You’ll be asked whether you’re providing console access to a person. It’s recommended to create users in IAM Identity Center rather than IAM. To switch to creating the user in IAM Identity Center, select Specify a user in Identity Center.
If IAM Identity Center is not enabled, this option takes you to the service page in the console to enable it. If IAM Identity Center is enabled, this option takes you to the Specify user details page in IAM Identity Center. If you cannot use IAM Identity Center, select I want to create an IAM user and continue following this procedure.
For Console password, choose one of the following:
Autogenerated password: The user gets a randomly generated password that adheres to the account password policy. You can view or download the password on the Retrieve password page. Custom password: Assign a password that you enter in the box. Optionally, select Users must create a new password at next sign-in (recommended) to ensure the user changes their password the first time they sign in.
Select Next.
On the Set permissions page, choose how to assign permissions for this user:
Add user to group: Assign the user to one or more groups with existing permissions policies. Copy permissions: Copy permissions from an existing user with similar needs. Attach policies directly: Attach AWS managed or custom policies directly to the user. It’s recommended to attach policies to groups whenever possible.
Optionally, set a permissions boundary in the Permissions boundary section. This is an advanced feature that controls maximum permissions.
Select Next.
Optionally, on the Review and create page, under Tags, you can attach metadata to the user using key-value pairs.
Review your choices, and when ready, select Create user.
On the Retrieve password page, get the password assigned to the user:
Select Show next to the password to view it manually.
Select Download .csv to save the user’s sign-in credentials as a .csv file.
Select Email sign-in instructions to customize and send an email to the user. The email includes their user name and a URL to the account sign-in page:
User name URL: https://AWS-account-ID-or-alias.signin.aws.amazon.com/console Note: The user’s password is not included in the email.
If the user also requires access keys, refer to Managing access keys for IAM users.
Login to AdminUser Return to the IAM service, and select Users in the left sidebar. Click on the name of the IAM User you just selected. In the Summary section, select the Security credentials tab. Look at the line Summary: Console sign-in link and copy the link next to it. This is the link you use to log in to the IAM User. Open an incognito tab of the browser you are using and paste the link into the search bar. Incognito tab login allows you to log in to AWS with an IAM User without having to log out of the root user in the main tab.
Enter the correct IAM User name and password that you entered in the create IAM User section above. Click sign in. Congratulations, you have successfully accessed your account as an IAM User AdminUser. In The next step, we will switch to using IAM Role to improve the security of your account. Creating Access Key for AWS Root User Minimum Required Permissions To perform the following steps, you need at least the following IAM (Identity and Access Management) permissions:
You must log in as the root user of AWS, which does not require any additional IAM permissions. These steps cannot be performed as an IAM user or a role.
Use the email address and password of your AWS account to sign in to the AWS Management Console as the root user.
In the top-right corner of the console, select your account name or number, then choose “Security Credentials”.
Under “Access keys,” select “Create access key.” If this option is unavailable, it means you have the maximum number of access keys. You must delete one of the existing access keys before creating a new one. For more information, see IAM Object Quotas in the IAM User Guide.
On the “Alternatives to root user access keys” page, consider security recommendations. To proceed, check the box and then select “Create access key.”
On the “Retrieve access key” page, your Access Key ID will be displayed.
Under the “Secret access key” section, select “Show,” then copy the Access Key ID and Secret Key from your browser window and paste them into a secure location. Alternatively, you can select “Download .csv file” to download a file named “rootkey.csv” containing the Access Key ID and Secret Key. Keep the file in a secure location.
Select “Done.” When you no longer need the access key, we recommend either deleting it or at least considering disabling it to prevent misuse.
Note: These steps apply only to the root user account on AWS. For IAM users or roles, the process of creating and managing access keys may differ.
Revoking Access Key for Root User on AWS Minimum Permissions To perform the following steps, you must have at least the following IAM (Identity and Access Management) permissions:
You must be logged in as the root user of your AWS account, this does not require any additional AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions. You cannot perform these steps as an IAM user or a role. Use the email address and password of your AWS account to sign in to the AWS Management Console as the root user. In the top-right corner of the console, select your account name or number, then choose Security Credentials. Under Access keys, select the access key you wish to delete, then in the Actions section, choose Delete. Note Alternatively, you can choose to Deactivate an access key instead of permanently deleting it. This allows you to continue using it in the future without changing both the key ID and secret key. While the key is deactivated, any requests using it in AWS API requests will fail with an “access denied” error.
In the Delete dialog, select Deactivate, enter the access key ID to confirm your intention to delete it, then choose Delete.

title: Monitoring Setup
content:
1. Objectives This section configures network traffic collection and email notifications.
The components include:
CloudWatch Logs stores traffic records. An IAM role allows VPC Flow Logs to publish logs. VPC Flow Logs collects accepted and rejected traffic. A metric filter counts rejected TCP 8080 records matching the lab conditions. A CloudWatch alarm evaluates the metric. Amazon SNS delivers notifications to the subscribed email address. Work in United States (N. Virginia) — us-east-1, consistent with the deployment in section 5.3.
If correctly configured resources already exist, inspect them and capture evidence.
2. Required Information Information Where to find it AWS account ID AWS account menu; 12 digits VPC ID VPC → Your VPCs EC2 public IPv4 EC2 → Instances → select the instance → Details EC2 private IPv4 The same Details tab Workshop client’s public IP Source of the HTTP rule in the security group Notification email An address where you can confirm the SNS subscription In the JSON examples, replace ACCOUNT_ID with your actual account ID.
In the filter pattern:
Replace CLIENT_PUBLIC_IP with the workshop client’s public IP, without /32. Replace EC2_PRIVATE_IP with the EC2 instance’s private IPv4 address. If you use a policy previously prepared for Singapore, update its Region conditions and ARNs containing a Region to us-east-1. IAM role ARNs do not contain a Region component.
3. Create the CloudWatch Log Group Open CloudWatch. Confirm that N. Virginia is selected. Open Log Management. If the console displays a Logs group, choose Logs → Log groups. Choose Create log group, or Actions → Create log group. Configure: Field Value Log group name /workshop/network/flowlogs Log class Standard Retention 7 days Choose Create. If retention was not configured during creation, return to the log group list, select the current value in the Retention column, and choose 7 days → Save.
The log group must use the Standard class to support metric filters.
Screenshot 1: Capture the log group name, log class, and retention after creation.
4. Create the VPC Flow Logs IAM Role 4.1. Configure the Trust Policy Open IAM → Roles → Create role. Choose Custom trust policy. Paste the following JSON and replace ACCOUNT_ID: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "vpc-flow-logs.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRole", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:SourceAccount": "ACCOUNT_ID" }, "ArnLike": { "aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:ec2:us-east-1:ACCOUNT_ID:vpc-flow-log/*" } } } ] } Choose Next. On Add permissions, continue without selecting a managed policy. Set Role name to workshop-flowlogs-role. Choose Create role. The trust policy allows VPC Flow Logs to assume the role and restricts the source to the lab’s account and Region.
If the role already exists, open Trust relationships → Edit trust policy to inspect or update it.
Screenshot 2: Capture the Trust relationships tab showing the service principal and source conditions.
4.2. Grant Log Publishing Permissions Open workshop-flowlogs-role. Choose Permissions → Add permissions → Create inline policy. Choose JSON. Paste the following and replace ACCOUNT_ID: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "PublishWorkshopFlowLogs", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "logs:CreateLogGroup", "logs:CreateLogStream", "logs:PutLogEvents", "logs:DescribeLogStreams" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:logs:us-east-1:ACCOUNT_ID:log-group:/workshop/network/flowlogs", "arn:aws:logs:us-east-1:ACCOUNT_ID:log-group:/workshop/network/flowlogs:*" ] }, { "Sid": "DescribeLogGroups", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "logs:DescribeLogGroups", "Resource": "*" } ] } Choose Next. Name the policy WorkshopFlowLogsPublish. Choose Create policy. If this inline policy already exists, edit the existing policy.
Screenshot 3: Capture the saved permissions policy in the role.
4.3. Verify PassRole Permissions The identity creating the flow log needs iam:PassRole permission for:
arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:role/workshop-flowlogs-role This permission belongs to the flow log creator. The service role’s permissions policy defines the log publishing operations the service can perform.
5. Create the VPC Flow Log Open VPC → Your VPCs. Select the workshop VPC. Choose Actions → Create flow log, or open Flow logs → Create flow log. Configure: Field Value Name, if shown aws-network-workshop-flowlogs Filter All Maximum aggregation interval 1 minute Destination Send to CloudWatch Logs Destination log group /workshop/network/flowlogs Service access Use an existing role IAM role workshop-flowlogs-role Log record format AWS default format Choose Create flow log. Verify the Active state and log delivery information. Keep AWS default format so the filter pattern in section 6 matches the field order.
Flow Logs requires time to aggregate and deliver data. A one-minute aggregation interval does not guarantee that records appear in CloudWatch within one minute.
Screenshot 4: Capture the flow log, its state, destination log group, and IAM role.
6. Create the Metric Filter 6.1. Enter the Filter Pattern Open CloudWatch → Log groups. Select /workshop/network/flowlogs. Choose Actions → Create metric filter. Enter the following Filter pattern on one line: [version, accountid, interfaceid, srcaddr = "CLIENT_PUBLIC_IP", dstaddr = "EC2_PRIVATE_IP", srcport, dstport = 8080, protocol = 6, packets, bytes, start, end, action = "REJECT", logstatus = "OK"] Replace both placeholders with actual IP addresses before creating the filter.
Condition Meaning srcaddr Workshop client’s public IP dstaddr EC2 private IPv4 dstport = 8080 Destination port used for testing protocol = 6 TCP action = "REJECT" Rejected traffic logstatus = "OK" Traffic record logged normally If matching logs already exist, you can use Test pattern to validate the filter. Distinguish pattern validation from the actual test evidence collected in section 5.5.
6.2. Configure the Metric Choose Next and enter:
Field Value Filter name rejected-tcp-8080 Metric namespace Workshop/Network Metric name Rejected8080Flows Metric value 1 Default value 0 Unit Count Dimensions Leave empty Choose Next → Create metric filter.
Each matching log record contributes a value of 1 to the metric.
Metric filters process new data after creation. The default value of 0 applies when logs are ingested but no records match; periods without log ingestion can still have missing data.
Screenshot 5: Capture the saved filter pattern, namespace, metric name, and metric value.
7. Create the SNS Topic and Email Subscription 7.1. Create the Topic Open Amazon SNS. Confirm that N. Virginia is selected. Choose Topics → Create topic. Enter: Field Value Type Standard Name aws-network-workshop-alerts Choose Create topic. 7.2. Subscribe an Email Address Open the topic. Choose Create subscription. Configure: Field Value Topic ARN The workshop topic Protocol Email Endpoint Your notification email address Choose Create subscription. Open the email from AWS Notifications. Select Confirm subscription. Return to SNS, refresh, and verify that the subscription is confirmed. Screenshot 6: Capture the confirmed subscription, with Pending confirmation no longer displayed.
7.3. Allow CloudWatch to Publish Notifications Open aws-network-workshop-alerts. Choose Edit → Access policy. Add the following object to the existing policy’s Statement array. Replace ACCOUNT_ID with your actual account ID. Preserve existing statements and separate the objects with commas. { "Sid": "AllowWorkshopAlarmPublish", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "cloudwatch.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": "sns:Publish", "Resource": "arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:ACCOUNT_ID:aws-network-workshop-alerts", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:SourceAccount": "ACCOUNT_ID" }, "ArnEquals": { "aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:cloudwatch:us-east-1:ACCOUNT_ID:alarm:aws-network-workshop-rejected-8080" } } } Choose Save changes. This statement allows the specified alarm to publish notifications to the topic.
Screenshot 7: Capture the saved access policy.
8. Create the CloudWatch Alarm 8.1. Select the Metric Open CloudWatch → Alarms → All alarms. Choose Create alarm → Select metric. Open the Workshop/Network namespace. Select the group without dimensions, usually shown as Metrics with no dimensions. Select Rejected8080Flows. Choose Select metric. If the metric is not visible, generate new data after creating the filter:
Keep port 8080 absent from the security group’s inbound allow rules. From the workshop client, try opening http://EC2_PUBLIC_IP:8080 several times, replacing EC2_PUBLIC_IP with the actual public IPv4. Wait for records to reach CloudWatch Logs and check the metric. Return to create the alarm. After creating the alarm, perform a new test in section 5.5 to correlate the test time, logs, metric, and email.
8.2. Configure the Condition Field Value Statistic Sum Period 5 minutes Threshold type Static Whenever metric is Greater/Equal Threshold value 1 Datapoints to alarm 1 out of 1 Missing data treatment Treat missing data as good (not breaching) The alarm condition is Sum >= 1 within a five-minute evaluation period.
Choose Next.
8.3. Configure Notifications Under Configure actions:
Field Value Alarm state trigger In alarm Send a notification to Select an existing SNS topic SNS topic aws-network-workshop-alerts Choose Next and enter:
Field Value Alarm name aws-network-workshop-rejected-8080 Description Notify when matching rejected TCP 8080 flow records are detected. Review the Preview page and choose Create alarm.
Screenshot 8: Capture the configured metric, alarm condition, and SNS action.
9. Evidence Checklist Image file Required content 01-log-group.png Log group name, Standard class, and retention 02-role-trust.png Flow Logs role trust policy 03-role-permissions.png Log publishing permissions policy 04-flow-log.png Flow log and destination configuration 05-metric-filter.png Filter pattern and metric 06-sns-subscription.png Confirmed email subscription 07-sns-policy.png Permission for CloudWatch to publish to SNS 08-alarm-config.png Alarm metric, threshold, and SNS action 10. Completion Checklist Regional services use us-east-1. The log group uses Standard class and seven-day retention. The IAM role has the correct trust and permissions policies. The flow log creator has the required PassRole permission. The flow log is Active and uses All traffic and AWS default format. The metric filter uses the correct source IP and private destination IP. The metric is Workshop/Network → Rejected8080Flows. The SNS email subscription is confirmed. The topic policy permits the alarm to publish. The alarm uses Sum, a threshold of >= 1, and the correct SNS topic. An OK state caused by missing-data handling does not establish that the complete monitoring chain is working.
Continue to 5.5 — Testing to correlate the connection, REJECT record, metric, ALARM state, and received email.
References AWS — Flow Logs IAM role AWS — Create a Flow Log to CloudWatch Logs AWS — Create a metric filter AWS — Creating metrics from log events AWS — Create a static threshold alarm AWS — Notify users on alarm changes

Building a Highly Secure Virtual Network Partition with Amazon VPC[cite: 3] Weekly Objectives Understand foundational networking concepts in AWS (CIDR blocks, Subnets, Route Tables). Design and implement a custom Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) from scratch. Securely separate resources using Public and Private subnets across multiple Availability Zones (AZs). Configure Internet Gateways (IGW) and NAT Gateways to manage inbound and outbound traffic. Implement a Bastion Host (Jump Box) for secure remote administration of private resources. Tasks Performed 1. Custom VPC and Subnet Architecture VPC Creation: Created a custom VPC with a specific IPv4 CIDR block (e.g., 10.0.0.0/16) to define an isolated virtual network. Subnetting: Segmented the VPC into multiple subnets to ensure high availability: Created two Public Subnets in different AZs (for resources needing direct internet access, like web servers). Created two Private Subnets in different AZs (for backend resources, like databases or application servers). 2. Traffic Routing and Gateways Internet Gateway (IGW): Created and attached an IGW to the custom VPC. Updated the main Route Table associated with the public subnets to route 0.0.0.0/0 traffic to the IGW, enabling internet access. NAT Gateway: Provisioned a NAT Gateway in one of the public subnets and allocated an Elastic IP. Configured the private subnets’ Route Table to direct outbound internet traffic (0.0.0.0/0) to the NAT Gateway, allowing private instances to download patches securely without receiving inbound traffic. 3. Security and Access Control Network ACLs (NACLs): Configured custom NACLs as a stateless firewall at the subnet level to explicitly allow or deny specific traffic. Bastion Host Deployment: Deployed a lightweight EC2 instance in the public subnet to act as a Bastion Host. Configured Security Groups so that the private instances only accept SSH traffic originating from the Bastion Host’s private IP. Achievements Successfully built a robust, enterprise-grade network topology mirroring real-world AWS best practices. Verified network isolation by successfully pinging the internet from a public instance, while confirming the private instance could only access the internet outbound via the NAT Gateway. Gained hands-on experience in troubleshooting routing issues and understanding the flow of traffic within a VPC. Challenges and Solutions Challenge: Instances launched in the private subnet could not access the internet to run yum update, even after creating the NAT Gateway. Solution: Discovered that creating the NAT Gateway is not enough; I had to manually edit the Route Table associated with the private subnet to add a route pointing destination 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT Gateway target. Once updated, outbound connectivity worked perfectly.

title: Testing and Validating the Monitoring System
content:
This section tests EC2 connectivity and validates the monitoring process from VPC Flow Logs through CloudWatch to Amazon SNS.
The following scenarios are used:
Scenario Expected result Access HTTP port 80 Successful connection and a working web page Connect to TCP port 8080 Failed connection and a matching REJECT flow log record A matching log record increases the CloudWatch metric. The alarm evaluates the metric against its configured threshold and sends an SNS notification when it transitions to ALARM.
1. Check the Prerequisites Use US East (N. Virginia) — us-east-1.
Verify the resources configured in section 5.4:
Resource Name EC2 instance aws-network-workshop-web Security group aws-network-workshop-web-sg Log group /workshop/network/flowlogs Metric filter rejected-tcp-8080 Metric namespace Workshop/Network Metric name Rejected8080Flows CloudWatch alarm aws-network-workshop-rejected-8080 SNS topic aws-network-workshop-alerts The instance must be Running. Its security groups must allow HTTP port 80 from the test client’s public IP address while keeping port 8080 blocked.
The examples use these addresses:
Address Value EC2 public IPv4 98.92.170.157 EC2 private IPv4 10.10.1.130 Test client public IP 1.55.6.233 Check the current addresses before testing. Update the examples and filter if any address has changed.
Check the test client’s public IP at:
https://checkip.amazonaws.com/
In the metric filter:
srcaddr must match the test client’s public IP without /32. dstaddr must match the EC2 private IPv4 address. The SNS email subscription must be confirmed. If the alarm is already in ALARM from an earlier test, stop generating test traffic and wait for it to return to OK before starting a new test.
2. Test HTTP Port 80 From the test client’s browser, open:
http://98.92.170.157 Enter the http:// scheme explicitly.
The expected result is the AWS Network Workshop page or the Nginx page served by the instance.
A successful response confirms that HTTP connectivity from the test client to the application is working.
3. Test TCP Port 8080 Open Windows PowerShell on the test client.
If you are using Command Prompt, enter the following command first:
powershell When the prompt starts with PS, run:
Get-Date Test-NetConnection -ComputerName 98.92.170.157 -Port 8080 Wait for the command to finish and inspect TcpTestSucceeded.
Expected result:
TcpTestSucceeded : False Repeat the test two or three more times if needed to generate traffic.
Record the test time so that you can compare it with the flow logs, metric data and alarm history.
Verify the failed connection against a matching REJECT record in the next step.
4. Verify the REJECT Flow Log Record In the AWS Console:
Open CloudWatch. Choose Logs → Log Management. Open /workshop/network/flowlogs. Select Log streams. Choose Search all log streams. Select the 1h time range. Enter this event filter:
[version, accountid, interfaceid, srcaddr = "1.55.6.233", dstaddr = "10.10.1.130", srcport, dstport = 8080, protocol = 6, packets, bytes, start, end, action = "REJECT", logstatus = "OK"] Replace the IP addresses if the current configuration differs.
Flow Logs require time to aggregate and deliver records. Delivery to CloudWatch typically takes about five minutes and may take longer. Choose Refresh to check for new records.
Expand a matching event using the arrow beside its timestamp.
Verify these fields:
Field Expected value srcaddr Test client’s public IP dstaddr EC2 private IPv4 dstport 8080 protocol 6, representing TCP action REJECT logstatus OK Use a record from the current test period. In the default flow log format, incoming traffic on the EC2 network interface uses its private IPv4 address as the destination.
Vietnam time is UTC plus seven hours.
5. Check the CloudWatch Metric In CloudWatch, open:
Metrics → Classic metrics
Under Browse, select:
Workshop/Network → Metrics with no dimensions
Select Rejected8080Flows, then open Graphed metrics.
Configure:
Setting Value Statistic Sum Period 5 minutes Time range 1h If the graph uses Average, change it to Sum to match the alarm configuration.
Choose Refresh and hover over a data point from the test period.
The expected result is a value of 1 or greater.
This metric counts matching log records. The number of connection attempts does not necessarily equal the metric value because Flow Logs aggregate traffic into records.
Metric filters process new data after creation and do not backfill existing logs.
6. Check the CloudWatch Alarm Open:
CloudWatch → Alarms → aws-network-workshop-rejected-8080
Verify:
Setting Value Namespace Workshop/Network Metric name Rejected8080Flows Statistic Sum Period 5 minutes Threshold >= 1 Datapoints to alarm 1 out of 1 Missing data treatment Treat missing data as good Actions Enabled When the data satisfies the configured condition, the expected state is In alarm.
Open History and compare the transition time with the test time.
If the alarm has already returned to OK, use the ALARM transition recorded in History to verify the earlier alert.
An OK state can be affected by missing data treatment. Compare the logs, metric and email notification to validate the complete process.
7. Verify the Amazon SNS Email Open the mailbox subscribed to aws-network-workshop-alerts.
Find the email containing:
aws-network-workshop-rejected-8080 Verify:
Alarm name. New state: ALARM. Notification time. Reason for the state change. If the email has not arrived:
Check the Spam or Junk folder. Verify that the subscription is confirmed. Check that the alarm action targets the correct SNS topic. Verify that the SNS access policy permits CloudWatch publishing. Inspect the alarm History for the action execution result. SNS does not send a new email for every connection attempt while the alarm remains in ALARM. A relevant state transition is required to trigger a new notification.
8. Completion Criteria Check each item after verifying and saving its evidence:
HTTP port 80 is accessible. TCP port 8080 connection fails. A REJECT record matches the test addresses, port and time. Rejected8080Flows has a Sum value of at least 1. The alarm transitions to ALARM during the test. The SNS alert email is received.

NETWORK AUTOMATION AND MONITORING ON AWS Introduction This workshop guides you through building a solution for automated infrastructure deployment and network monitoring on AWS.
The solution uses Terraform to deploy infrastructure, VPC Flow Logs to collect network traffic information, Amazon CloudWatch to analyze logs and monitor activity, and Amazon SNS to deliver email alerts.
The content is organized into separate sections, allowing you to progress from environment preparation to deployment, testing, and resource cleanup.
AWS Region: ap-southeast-1 (Singapore). Use the same Region throughout this workshop.
Objectives After completing this workshop, you will be able to:
Create a VPC with public and private subnets. Configure route tables and Security Groups. Deploy an Nginx web server on Amazon EC2. Automate infrastructure provisioning with Terraform. Collect network traffic information using VPC Flow Logs. Analyze logs and monitor metrics with Amazon CloudWatch. Configure email alerts using Amazon SNS. Test the solution and remove resources after the exercises. Workshop Contents Section Topic Description 5.1 Overview Problem statement, system architecture, and traffic flow 5.2 Preparation AWS account, IAM permissions, and required tools 5.3 Infrastructure Automation Write Terraform configuration for AWS resources 5.4 System-Deployment Validate configuration, create resources, and confirm SNS 5.5 Testing and Alerts Verify connectivity, logs, and email alerts 5.6 Analysisand Monitoring Query logs and inspect the CloudWatch dashboard 5.7 Troubleshooting Identify and resolve common issues 5.8 Resultsand Evidence Record test results and capture screenshots 5.9 Resource Cleanup Delete resources created during the workshop Expected Results After implementation, the solution should:
Deploy AWS infrastructure from Terraform configuration. Serve the Nginx web page to the allowed source IP address. Record accepted and rejected network traffic. Display network metrics on a CloudWatch dashboard. Send an email when the number of matching rejected-flow records reaches the configured alarm threshold. Note: AWS resources may incur charges. Remove the resources after completing the exercises.

Designing ERD and Provisioning Amazon RDS PostgreSQL Database[cite: 3] Weekly Objectives Understand the fundamentals of relational database design and normalization. Create an Entity-Relationship Diagram (ERD) to map out the data architecture for a sample application. Provision and configure a managed relational database using Amazon RDS with the PostgreSQL engine. Implement database security best practices, including network isolation and strict Security Group rules. Successfully connect to the RDS instance and perform basic SQL operations. Tasks Performed 1. Database Design and ERD Creation Requirement Analysis: Analyzed the data requirements for a sample e-commerce application (Users, Products, Orders, Order Items). ERD Modeling: Used database design tools (e.g., dbdiagram.io or draw.io) to draw the ERD. Defined primary keys (PK), foreign keys (FK), data types, and relationships (1:N, M:N) between tables to ensure data integrity and minimize redundancy. 2. Provisioning Amazon RDS Instance Setup: Navigated to the RDS Console and created a standard PostgreSQL database instance. Selected the Free Tier eligible db.t3.micro instance class. Storage & Authentication: Configured allocated storage (20GB General Purpose SSD) and disabled storage autoscaling to control costs. Set up the master username and generated a strong, secure master password. 3. Network and Security Configuration Subnet Groups: Created an RDS Subnet Group spanning multiple Availability Zones within the Private Subnets created in Week 4, ensuring the database is not publicly accessible. Security Groups: Created a dedicated Security Group for the RDS instance. Configured the Inbound Rule to only allow PostgreSQL traffic (Port 5432) originating from the Application Security Group (or the Bastion Host Security Group) to prevent unauthorized access. 4. Database Connection and Testing Client Connection: Retrieved the RDS endpoint from the AWS Console. Used a database client (pgAdmin and psql CLI) installed on an EC2 instance in the public subnet to connect to the database. Database Initialization: Executed DDL (Data Definition Language) scripts to create the tables based on the ERD and inserted sample data using DML (Data Manipulation Language) queries. Achievements Successfully translated business logic into a structured relational database schema. Deployed a fully managed, secure PostgreSQL database inside a private network, adhering to AWS security standards. Verified seamless and secure communication between the application tier (EC2) and the database tier (RDS). Challenges and Solutions Challenge: Encountered a Connection timed out error when attempting to connect to the RDS endpoint from my local machine using pgAdmin. Solution: Realized that placing the RDS instance in a Private Subnet and setting “Public access” to “No” means it cannot be accessed directly from the internet. I resolved this by using SSH Port Forwarding (SSH Tunneling) through the Bastion Host (EC2) to securely route my local pgAdmin connection to the private RDS endpoint.

title: Dashboard and Network Log Analysis
content:
In this section, we build a CloudWatch dashboard that brings network monitoring information together on one screen.
The dashboard contains three components:
Component Purpose Rejected8080Flows graph Monitor rejected port 8080 flow records over time Alarm status widget Display the alarm’s current state ACCEPT/REJECT table Summarize flow records by action and destination port We also use CloudWatch Logs Insights to analyze VPC Flow Logs and add the query results to the dashboard.
1. Prerequisites Use US East (N. Virginia) — us-east-1 when selecting the workshop metrics and logs.
Verify the following resources:
Resource Value Log group /workshop/network/flowlogs Metric namespace Workshop/Network Metric name Rejected8080Flows Alarm aws-network-workshop-rejected-8080 Test data from section 5.5 is required to populate the graph and query results.
The sample query uses:
Address Value Test client’s public IP 1.55.6.233 EC2 private IPv4 10.10.1.130 Update the query if either address has changed.
2. Create a CloudWatch Dashboard Open CloudWatch. Choose Dashboards in the navigation pane. If the navigation pane is hidden, open it using the ☰ icon. Choose Create dashboard. Enter: aws-network-workshop-dashboard Choose Create dashboard. The console opens the widget configuration dialog for the first dashboard component.
3. Add the Rejected8080Flows Graph In Add widget, select:
Setting Value Data sources types CloudWatch Data type Metrics Preferred experience Metrics Console Widget type Line Choose Next.
In the metric selector:
Open Browse. Select Workshop/Network. Choose Metrics with no dimensions, if displayed. Select Rejected8080Flows. Open Graphed metrics. Configure:
Setting Value Statistic Sum Period 5 minutes Time range 3h, or a range containing the test If the statistic is Average, change it to Sum. This displays the total value for each five-minute period and matches the alarm configuration.
Screenshot 01: Capture the metric configuration showing Rejected8080Flows, Sum and a five-minute period.
Choose Create widget, then Save dashboard.
4. Add the Alarm Status Widget On the dashboard:
Choose Add widget or the + icon. Keep CloudWatch as the data source. Under Data type, choose Alarms, beside Metrics and Logs. Select Alarm status. Choose Next, if displayed. Find and select: aws-network-workshop-rejected-8080 Complete the dialog using Create widget or Add to dashboard, as displayed. Choose Save dashboard. The widget displays the alarm’s current state:
State Meaning OK The alarm is not breaching under its configured evaluation settings ALARM The alarm is in its alert state INSUFFICIENT_DATA There is insufficient data for evaluation The state changes with the evaluated data. Selecting a historical dashboard time range does not make this widget display a historical alarm state.
Screenshot 02: Capture the alarm widget showing its name and current state.
5. Analyze ACCEPT and REJECT Records In the CloudWatch navigation pane, open:
Logs → Log Analytics
Log Analytics brings together log analysis capabilities, including Logs Insights.
5.1. Select the Query Scope Under Query scope:
Choose All beside Log group. Select: /workshop/network/flowlogs Keep Log class = Standard. Select 3h, or use Custom to include the test period from section 5.5. Use Logs Insights QL. The default query containing fields, sort and limit in this interface already uses this language.
5.2. Enter the Query In the new interface, keep the first line beginning with SOURCE, if present. Replace the query from the fields line onward with:
fields srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort, protocol, action, logStatus | filter srcAddr = "1.55.6.233" and dstAddr = "10.10.1.130" and protocol = 6 and logStatus = "OK" | filter dstPort = 80 or dstPort = 8080 | stats count(*) as FlowRecords by action, dstPort | sort dstPort asc This query:
Filters traffic from the test client’s public IP to the EC2 private IP. Selects TCP records with an OK logging status. Limits destination ports to 80 and 8080. Groups records by action and destination port. Counts the records in each group. Choose Run or Run query.
5.3. Interpret the Results The results contain:
Column Meaning action ACCEPT or REJECT dstPort Destination port FlowRecords Matching record count within the selected time range When corresponding test traffic exists, the results can include ACCEPT on port 80 and REJECT on port 8080.
FlowRecords counts flow log records, rather than page refreshes or individual packets.
If no results appear, check:
The selected log group. Whether the time range includes the test. Both IP addresses in the query. Whether Flow Logs have delivered the records. Screenshot 03: Capture the selected log group, query text and results table.
6. Add the Query Results to the Dashboard After the query completes successfully:
Choose Add to dashboard. Select: aws-network-workshop-dashboard Choose the Table widget type. Enter the widget name: ACCEPT and REJECT by port Choose Add to dashboard. Return to the dashboard and choose Save dashboard. The query table summarizes records across the selected time range. The metric graph shows individual five-minute periods and monitors only rejected port 8080 traffic.
7. Arrange and Verify the Dashboard Open:
CloudWatch → Dashboards → aws-network-workshop-dashboard
Arrange the components:
Rejected8080Flows graph at the top. Alarm status widget beside the graph. ACCEPT and REJECT by port table below. Drag a widget corner to resize it and drag its title area to reposition it.
Select a time range containing the test and choose Refresh. Choose Save dashboard after changing the layout.
Verify that the dashboard displays:
Metric data in the graph. The alarm name and current state. The ACCEPT/REJECT results table. Screenshot 04: Capture the full dashboard, including its name and all three widgets.
8. Completion Criteria The aws-network-workshop-dashboard dashboard is created and saved. The graph uses Rejected8080Flows. The statistic is Sum and the period is five minutes. The alarm widget displays the correct name and current state. The Logs Insights query returns appropriate data. The results table is added to the dashboard. The required evidence screenshots are captured.
