Openness to guidance: Adjusted my approach after receiving explanations. Attention to documentation: Worked on Markdown content, English versions, and supporting screenshot placement. Commitment to improvement: Continued exploring subsequent sections to develop a more complete workshop. Areas for Improvement 1. Understand Concepts Before Applying Configurations I need to strengthen my understanding of IP addresses, CIDR, subnets, routing, and Security Groups. For IAM, I need to distinguish permission policies, trust policies, and iam:PassRole.
Understanding the purpose of each configuration will help me work more independently.
2. Improve Research and Troubleshooting Skills Before requesting assistance, I should review the instructions, read error messages, and check the values I entered.
I should also record the causes of problems and their solutions so that I can handle similar issues independently.
3. Communicate More Clearly When asking for help, I should explain the current step, the actions already performed, the actual result, and the expected result.
Screenshots should clearly show the relevant information.
4. Track Progress and Verify Results I should divide the workshop into smaller tasks, define completion criteria, and verify each task separately.

Development Goals Repeat the workshop with less guidance. Explain the function and purpose of each resource independently. Maintain notes about common errors and solutions. Complete the report with screenshots that reflect actual results. Seek opportunities to practice with others and develop teamwork skills. After mastering the fundamentals, explore AWS CloudFormation or Terraform.

Researching High Availability and Scalable Distributed Architecture Solutions[cite: 3] 1. Problem Statement & Architecture Evolution In previous weeks, the architecture relied on a single EC2 instance. If that instance failed or an Availability Zone (AZ) went down, the entire application would crash (Single Point of Failure - SPOF). The objective of Week 6 is to design and implement a Highly Available (HA) and Scalable architecture that can automatically self-heal and scale based on user traffic.
2. Core Components Researched Elastic Load Balancing (ELB): Deep dive into Application Load Balancer (ALB) for Layer 7 HTTP/HTTPS traffic routing, SSL termination, and continuous instance health checking. Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling: Understanding Launch Templates, Auto Scaling Groups (ASG), and dynamic scaling policies (Target Tracking, Step Scaling). Database HA: Researching Amazon RDS Multi-AZ deployments for synchronous data replication and automatic failover. 3. Proof of Concept (PoC) Implementation To validate the theories, I built a PoC distributed environment:
Golden AMI Creation: Configured a baseline EC2 instance with all necessary application dependencies, then baked it into a custom Amazon Machine Image (AMI) to ensure consistency across newly spawned instances. Launch Template Configuration: Created a Launch Template specifying the Golden AMI, t2.micro instance type, and the required IAM Role, ensuring instances boot up ready-to-serve. ALB & Target Group Setup: Provisioned an internet-facing ALB across two Public Subnets. Configured a Target Group spanning two Private Subnets and set up strict health checks (/health path returning HTTP 200). Auto Scaling Group (ASG): Attached the ASG to the ALB Target Group. Set the capacity limits: Minimum = 2, Desired = 2, Maximum = 4 instances across multi-AZs. 4. Chaos Engineering & Stress Testing Instead of just deploying, I actively tried to “break” the system to observe its behavior:
Chaos Test (Instance Termination): Manually terminated one of the running EC2 instances from the console. Result: The ALB immediately detected the failure via health checks, stopped routing traffic to the dead node, and the ASG automatically spun up a replacement instance within 2 minutes to restore the desired capacity. Stress Test (Load Spiking): SSH-ed into an instance and used the Linux stress utility (stress --cpu 4 --timeout 300) to artificially spike CPU utilization above 75%. Result: The CloudWatch Alarm triggered the ASG Target Tracking policy, automatically launching two new instances to handle the simulated traffic surge. 5. Key Takeaways & Challenges Takeaway: A distributed architecture significantly enhances reliability. Users experience zero downtime even if underlying hardware fails. Challenge: Session management became an issue. When ALB routed a user to a new instance, they were logged out. Solution: Researched and applied “Sticky Sessions” on the ALB and began exploring external session storage using Amazon ElastiCache (Redis) to truly decouple state from the application servers.

title: Troubleshooting the Monitoring System
content:
This section explains how to diagnose issues involving VPC Flow Logs, CloudWatch metrics, alarms and Amazon SNS.
Each scenario follows this structure:
Symptom. Cause. Investigation and resolution. Verification evidence. Previously captured error screenshots can be compared with the configuration and results after correction.
1. Preparation Use US East (N. Virginia) — us-east-1 when checking the workshop resources.
Resource Name Flow Logs IAM role workshop-flowlogs-role Log group /workshop/network/flowlogs Metric filter rejected-tcp-8080 Metric namespace Workshop/Network Metric name Rejected8080Flows Alarm aws-network-workshop-rejected-8080 SNS topic aws-network-workshop-alerts Before repeating a test, verify the client’s public IP and the EC2 addresses.
Check the client’s public IP at:
https://checkip.amazonaws.com/
If it has changed, update the HTTP security group rule’s Source and the metric filter’s srcaddr.
2. Workshop/Network Metric Is Missing 2.1. Symptom The metric selector does not display the Workshop/Network namespace or Rejected8080Flows metric.
2.2. Possible Causes The metric filter has not been created. Configuration was entered but not saved. The namespace or metric name is incorrect. No data points have been published. The filter does not match the test traffic. 2.3. Investigation and Resolution Open:
CloudWatch → Logs → Log Management → /workshop/network/flowlogs → Metric filters
If the page shows Metric filters (0), create the metric filter.
If the filter exists, select rejected-tcp-8080 → Edit and verify:
Setting Value Filter name rejected-tcp-8080 Metric namespace Workshop/Network Metric name Rejected8080Flows Metric value 1 Default value 0 Dimensions Leave empty Compare the filter pattern with:
[version, accountid, interfaceid, srcaddr = "1.55.6.233", dstaddr = "10.10.1.130", srcport, dstport = 8080, protocol = 6, packets, bytes, start, end, action = "REJECT", logstatus = "OK"] In this example:
1.55.6.233 is the test client’s public IP. 10.10.1.130 is the EC2 private IPv4 address. Replace these addresses if they have changed. Do not append /32 to srcaddr.
Complete the save steps, then generate new test traffic to port 8080.
Metric filters process new data after creation and do not backfill existing logs.
Screenshot 01: Capture the saved metric filter and its metric settings.
3. The Graph Uses Average Instead of Sum 3.1. Symptom The graph displays fractional values while the intended view is the total count of matching records.
3.2. Cause The graph’s statistic is set to Average.
Average represents the mean value. Sum represents the total value within the selected period.
3.3. Investigation and Resolution Open:
CloudWatch → Metrics → Classic metrics
Select:
Workshop/Network → Metrics with no dimensions → Rejected8080Flows
Under Graphed metrics, configure:
Setting Value Statistic Sum Period 5 minutes Time range A range containing the test Choose Refresh and hover over a data point to inspect its value.

Researching Ultra-Low Latency Global Content Delivery via Amazon CloudFront (CDN)[cite: 3] 1. Problem Statement: The Global Latency Bottleneck Following the highly available architecture established in Week 6, our application was robust but physically bound to a single AWS Region (ap-southeast-1, Singapore). When testing access from North America or Europe, network latency spiked significantly (250-300ms) due to geographical distance. Loading heavy static assets (high-res images, videos, heavy JavaScript bundles) became a bottleneck. The objective of Week 7 is to implement Amazon CloudFront to deliver content globally with ultra-low latency.
2. Core Concepts & Services Researched Amazon CloudFront (CDN): Deep dive into how Edge Locations and Regional Edge Caches work to cache content closer to end-users. Origin Access Control (OAC): Replaces the legacy Origin Access Identity (OAI) to securely restrict direct public access to S3 buckets, ensuring users must go through CloudFront. AWS Certificate Manager (ACM): Provisioning SSL/TLS certificates for data-in-transit encryption. Cache Behaviors & Time-To-Live (TTL): Understanding how to configure caching rules based on URL paths and HTTP headers. 3. Proof of Concept (PoC) & Implementation I architected a multi-origin CloudFront distribution to handle both static and dynamic content:
Static Asset Delivery (S3 Origin): Created a dedicated S3 bucket for static media (/assets, /images). Configured CloudFront to use this S3 bucket as an origin. Implemented OAC (Origin Access Control) and updated the S3 Bucket Policy to explicitly allow s3:GetObject only from the specific CloudFront Distribution ARN. Direct S3 endpoint access was strictly blocked. Dynamic Traffic Routing (ALB Origin): Added the Application Load Balancer (ALB) from Week 6 as a second origin. Configured Cache Behaviors: Path Default (*): Forwarded to ALB with caching disabled (forwarding all headers, cookies, and query strings) to ensure dynamic application logic (like logins) works perfectly. Path /assets/*: Routed to the S3 bucket with heavy caching enabled (TTL set to 24 hours). Custom Domain & SSL Setup: Requested a public SSL certificate via ACM. (Crucial Note: The certificate had to be requested in the us-east-1 N. Virginia region to be attachable to CloudFront). Configured Amazon Route 53 to map a custom domain (e.g., app.myproject.com) to the CloudFront distribution using an Alias record. 4. Performance Benchmarking I used browser DevTools (Network tab) and online tools (Pingdom) to measure the impact:
Before CDN: Downloading a 3MB background image from the US took ~1.2 seconds. After CDN (Cache HIT): The same image loaded in ~80 milliseconds from a local US Edge Location. The X-Cache header in the HTTP response clearly showed Hit from cloudfront. 5. Key Takeaways & Challenges Resolved Challenge 1 - Cache Stale Data: I deployed a new CSS update, but users were still seeing the old design. Resolution: Learned about the “Cache Invalidation” process. I manually triggered an invalidation for /* in the CloudFront console. To avoid invalidation costs in the future, I researched the best practice of “File Versioning” (e.g., style.v2.css). Challenge 2 - CORS Errors: Web fonts loaded via CloudFront were blocked by Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) policies. Resolution: Updated the S3 CORS configuration to allow GET requests from my custom domain and configured CloudFront to forward the Origin, Access-Control-Request-Headers, and Access-Control-Request-Method headers.

This section consolidates evidence and evaluates the AWS network monitoring implementation.
The evaluation uses actual data from:
Connectivity tests. VPC Flow Logs. CloudWatch metrics and alarms. Amazon SNS alert emails. The monitoring dashboard. Troubleshooting results. Screenshots from previous sections can be reused when they contain the information required for evaluation.
1. Prepare the Evaluation Use US East (N. Virginia) — us-east-1 when opening metrics, logs and alarms.
Review the following resources:
Resource Value Log group /workshop/network/flowlogs Metric namespace Workshop/Network Metric name Rejected8080Flows Alarm aws-network-workshop-rejected-8080 SNS topic aws-network-workshop-alerts Dashboard aws-network-workshop-dashboard Select one test run from section 5.5 for comparison.
Check source and destination addresses, ports and timestamps to ensure that the evidence belongs to the same test run.
2. Review the Monitoring Dashboard Open:
CloudWatch → Dashboards → aws-network-workshop-dashboard
Select a time range containing the test and choose Refresh.
Verify the three components:
Component What to Verify Metric graph Rejected8080Flows contains test data, using Sum and a five-minute period Alarm status The correct alarm name and its current state Log analysis table Appropriate results in action, dstPort and FlowRecords The alarm status widget displays the current state. The alarm may have returned to OK after the test.
Use the alarm History to verify the earlier alert rather than relying solely on the dashboard’s current status.
Screenshot 01: Capture the dashboard name and all three widgets.
3. Assess the Test Results Use one of these statuses:
Pass: Evidence satisfies the criterion. Fail: The item was checked and did not satisfy the criterion. Not verified: There is insufficient evidence to conclude. Complete the Result column after reviewing the evidence.
Item Pass Criterion Evidence Result Application access HTTP port 80 displays the web page Browser screenshot — Connection control TCP port 8080 connection fails PowerShell result — Log collection A record matches the test addresses, port 8080, REJECT and OK Expanded flow log record — Metric generation Rejected8080Flows has a Sum of at least 1 during the test Metric graph — Alarm activation The alarm transitions to ALARM based on test data Alarm History — Notification delivery An alert email contains the alarm name and corresponding time SNS alert email — Centralized visibility The dashboard is saved and contains all three widgets Dashboard screenshot — The direct message titled Workshop 5.7 - SNS delivery test verifies SNS email delivery.
To evaluate the CloudWatch notification path, use the email containing the alarm name and ALARM state from the selected test.
4. Compare Timestamps and Evaluate Latency 4.1. Collect the Timestamps Open:
CloudWatch → Alarms → aws-network-workshop-rejected-8080 → History
Find the ALARM transition for the selected test and record its time.
Compare these timestamps:
Timestamp Meaning Source Actual Value T0 Test start time Get-Date or the time recorded in section 5.5 — T_flow Flow record time Timestamp in CloudWatch Logs — T_alarm ALARM transition time Alarm History — T_email Email receipt time Subscribed mailbox — Use the same time zone when comparing timestamps.
Vietnam time = UTC + 7 hours The CloudWatch timestamp of a flow log record corresponds to the flow’s start time. The time CloudWatch receives the record is a separate timestamp.
Use the actual recorded T0 when measuring latency from the beginning of the test.
Screenshot 02: Capture the alarm name, ALARM transition and timestamp in History.
4.2. Calculate Latency When sufficient data is available, calculate:
Alarm latency = T_alarm - T0 Email receipt latency = T_email - T0 Record the measurements:
Measurement Actual Result Alarm latency — Email receipt latency — If T0 or another required timestamp was not recorded, enter Not measured for the corresponding measurement.
Match the reported precision to the available evidence. If the mailbox displays only minutes, do not report second-level precision.
Screenshot 03: Capture the alert email showing its alarm name, ALARM state and time.
5. Evaluate System Capabilities Compare the evidence with the following capabilities:
Capability Evaluation Traffic control Security groups apply the configured access rules Automated collection Flow Logs record and deliver network data to CloudWatch Logs Monitoring data generation The metric filter converts matching records into data points Automated alerting The alarm evaluates its threshold and invokes actions on state changes Notification delivery SNS delivers notifications to the confirmed email subscription Centralized visibility The dashboard combines metrics, alarm status and log analysis Troubleshooting Logs Insights supports filtering and summarizing test data Mark a capability as verified only when supporting evidence is available.
Infrastructure in this workshop is provisioned through the AWS Console. The configured automation covers log collection, metric generation, alarm evaluation and notification delivery.
6. Record the Limitations 6.1. Filter Scope The metric filter monitors specific source and destination addresses and destination port 8080.
Update the filter when an address changes.
6.2. Delivery Latency Flow Logs require aggregation and delivery time. A one-minute aggregation interval does not guarantee that the complete alerting process finishes within one minute.
6.3. Interpretation of Counts Rejected8080Flows counts matching log records.
The record count can differ from connection attempts, page refreshes or packet counts because traffic is aggregated into flow records.
6.4. New and Missing Data Metric filters process new data after creation and do not backfill existing logs.
Missing data treatment can affect an alarm’s OK state. Compare logs, metrics, alarm history and emails to evaluate the complete process.
6.5. Notification Conditions Alarm notifications are triggered by relevant state transitions. Additional test connections do not create a new email while the alarm remains in ALARM.
7. Record the Findings Complete this table using actual results:
Item Findings Items verified as passed — Failed or unverified items — Measured latency, if available — Issues encountered and their resolutions — Limitations of the current configuration — Improvements to consider — 8. Completion Criteria Evidence from the same test run is compared. The evaluation table reflects actual results. Available timestamps are recorded with supporting evidence. Measurements lacking sufficient data are marked Not measured. System capabilities and limitations are assessed. Required evidence screenshots are saved. After completing the evaluation and saving the evidence, continue to 5.9 — Resource Cleanup.

Reviewing Architecture Diagrams, Configuring AWS Budgets, IAM Roles, and Baseline CloudFront[cite: 3] 1. Weekly Objectives: Consolidation & Security Hardening After several weeks of rapidly deploying new services (EC2, VPC, RDS, ALB, S3, CloudFront), Week 8 serves as a crucial consolidation phase. The primary goals are to map out the current infrastructure visually, enforce the Principle of Least Privilege using IAM Roles, implement strict cost controls to avoid unexpected billing surprises, and fine-tune the baseline CDN configurations.
2. Core Tasks & Implementation 2.1. Architecture Diagram Review Visualizing the Infrastructure: Used diagramming tools (Draw.io / AWS Architecture Icons) to create a comprehensive, high-level architecture diagram. Component Mapping: Documented the traffic flow starting from the end-user -> Amazon Route 53 -> CloudFront -> Internet Gateway -> Application Load Balancer -> Auto Scaling Group (EC2) -> Amazon RDS (Private Subnet). Security Boundary Verification: Reviewed the Security Group matrix to ensure there are no open ports (0.0.0.0/0) except for HTTP/HTTPS on the Load Balancer and Bastion Host (port 22, restricted to my IP). 2.2. Enforcing IAM Roles (Replacing Access Keys) Security Audit: Identified that some EC2 instances were previously using hardcoded AWS Access Keys via aws configure to interact with S3. This is a major security risk. IAM Instance Profiles: Created a custom IAM Role for EC2 with a strict policy allowing only s3:PutObject and s3:GetObject to a specific bucket. Attached this IAM Role (Instance Profile) to the Auto Scaling Group’s Launch Template. Removed all local AWS credentials from the instances. Verified that the EC2 instances could still seamlessly interact with S3 using temporary, auto-rotating credentials provided by the IAM Role. 2.3. Configuring AWS Budgets & Cost Optimization Cost Analysis: Reviewed the AWS Billing Dashboard to analyze the cost accumulation from the NAT Gateway, ALB, and RDS running 24/7. Budget Alarms: Configured an AWS Cost Budget with a hard limit of $20.00 for the month. Set up multiple alert thresholds (e.g., at 50%, 80%, and 100% of the budgeted amount) to trigger email notifications via Amazon SNS. Identified unused EBS snapshots and unattached Elastic IPs, deleting them to halt unnecessary charges. 2.4. Baseline CloudFront Tuning Geo-Restriction: Implemented geographic restrictions on the CloudFront distribution to block traffic from specific countries where the application has no target audience, mitigating potential basic DDoS attempts. AWS WAF Integration (Overview): Began reviewing the integration of AWS Web Application Firewall (WAF) with CloudFront to block malicious requests (like SQL injection or Cross-Site Scripting) at the edge before they reach the ALB. 3. Key Takeaways & Challenges Takeaway: IAM Roles are significantly more secure and easier to manage at scale compared to static Access Keys. Visualizing the architecture helped identify a redundant NAT Gateway that was silently accumulating costs. Challenge: After attaching the IAM Role to the EC2 instances, the application still threw an Access Denied error when trying to upload files to S3. Resolution: Investigated the IAM Policy logic and discovered that while the EC2 had the correct IAM Role, the S3 Bucket Policy (configured in Week 7 for CloudFront OAC) was implicitly denying all other traffic. I had to update the Bucket Policy to explicitly allow the new EC2 IAM Role’s ARN.

Standardizing and Packaging Infrastructure Codebase and Integrating Team Workflows[cite: 3] 1. Weekly Objectives: Moving from Click-Ops to GitOps After building a robust architecture manually via the AWS Management Console over the past weeks, the goal of Week 9 is to automate the entire provisioning process. The objectives include adopting Infrastructure as Code (IaC), establishing version control best practices for team collaboration, and building a foundational Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline.
2. Core Tasks & Implementation 2.1. Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Implementation Code Standardization: Chose AWS CloudFormation (or Terraform) to declare the infrastructure setup. Translated the manually configured VPC, Subnets, Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway, and Security Groups into a standardized YAML/HCL template. Modularization: Instead of writing one massive file, I refactored the codebase into reusable modules (e.g., separating the Networking stack from the Database and Compute stacks) to make it easier to maintain and update. 2.2. Version Control & Team Workflows Git Integration: Initialized a Git repository (using AWS CodeCommit or GitHub) to centrally manage the IaC templates and application source code. Branching Strategy: Implemented a standard Git workflow (Feature Branching). Created main, staging, and dev branches to simulate a real-world team environment where infrastructure changes must be reviewed via Pull Requests (PRs) before merging. 2.3. CI/CD Pipeline Automation AWS CodePipeline & CodeBuild: Configured a continuous delivery pipeline. Source Stage: Hooked the pipeline to the Git repository to trigger automatically upon new commits to the main branch. Build/Test Stage: Used AWS CodeBuild to run a syntax linter (cfn-lint or tflint) to validate the infrastructure code before deployment. Deploy Stage: Configured the pipeline to automatically deploy or update the CloudFormation stack, ensuring the cloud environment strictly matches the codebase. 3. Key Takeaways & Challenges Takeaway: IaC is a game-changer. Rebuilding the entire Week 4-6 architecture now takes minutes instead of hours, and the environment is 100% reproducible and self-documenting. Challenge: Encountered a “Stack Drift” issue where a manual change made directly in the AWS Console (to fix a quick bug) caused the CloudFormation stack update to fail because the code state and the physical cloud state were out of sync. Resolution: Learned that when using IaC, all changes must go through the code pipeline. I used the CloudFormation Drift Detection feature to identify the manual changes, updated my code to match the new reality, and successfully synced the stack.

Participating in System Integration Testing, Network Verification, and Troubleshooting[cite: 3] 1. Weekly Objectives: Ensuring System Reliability With the infrastructure fully automated via IaC and CI/CD pipelines (completed in Week 9), the primary goal of Week 10 is to validate that all interconnected components function together seamlessly as a unified system. This involves System Integration Testing (SIT), verifying network routing, and proactively troubleshooting simulated infrastructure failures.
2. Core Tasks & Implementation 2.1. End-to-End System Integration Testing (SIT) Traffic Flow Validation: Conducted end-to-end testing by simulating real user traffic. Verified the flow from CloudFront (CDN) -> Application Load Balancer -> Auto Scaling Group (EC2) -> RDS PostgreSQL database. Application Logic Testing: Deployed a sample web application to test database read/write operations (e.g., submitting a mock order) to ensure the application servers in the private subnets could successfully communicate with the RDS instance. 2.2. Network Verification & Monitoring VPC Flow Logs: Enabled VPC Flow Logs and routed the data to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Analyzed the logs to monitor ACCEPT and REJECT traffic patterns, providing deep visibility into what IP addresses were attempting to access the resources. VPC Reachability Analyzer: Utilized the AWS Network Access Analyzer and Reachability Analyzer to mathematically verify connectivity between the Internet Gateway and the EC2 instances, ensuring there were no unintended network paths bypassing the Load Balancer. 2.3. Failover & Disaster Recovery Testing RDS Multi-AZ Failover: Manually triggered a “Reboot with failover” on the primary RDS instance. Observation: Monitored the application’s downtime. The system automatically updated the DNS endpoint to point to the standby replica in a different Availability Zone. The application reconnected successfully within ~60 seconds, proving the high availability of the database tier. 3. Key Takeaways & Challenges Takeaway: Advanced network monitoring tools like VPC Flow Logs and Reachability Analyzer are invaluable for diagnosing complex routing and security group issues without needing to SSH into individual servers. Challenge: During the integration test, the EC2 instances could connect to the database, but they intermittently failed to download external API payloads. Resolution: By querying the VPC Flow Logs using CloudWatch Logs Insights, I discovered that return traffic was being dropped. I realized the NAT Gateway in one of the Availability Zones was misconfigured in the private subnet’s Route Table. Correcting the route entry immediately resolved the intermittent timeout issues.

Consolidating Screenshots, Contributions, and Proofreading the Final Report[cite: 3] 1. Weekly Objectives: Documentation & Technical Communication After 10 weeks of intense cloud infrastructure deployment and testing, Week 11 is dedicated to technical writing and project documentation. The primary goal is to synthesize all practical work, gather concrete visual evidence (screenshots, metrics, diagrams), articulate personal technical contributions clearly, and format the final report using the Hugo static site generator to ensure a professional, web-ready presentation.
2. Core Tasks & Implementation 2.1. Evidence Collection & Visual Documentation Console & CLI Screenshots: Captured high-quality screenshots of critical AWS configurations as proof of work. This included the VPC Resource Map, running EC2 instances across multi-AZs, ALB target group health checks (showing Healthy status), and RDS database connectivity. Metrics & Dashboards: Extracted CloudWatch metric graphs demonstrating the Auto Scaling Group’s response to the CPU stress tests conducted in Week 6, providing empirical data to support the High Availability (HA) claims. Final Architecture Diagram: Updated the initial system architecture diagram using Draw.io to accurately reflect the final deployed state, explicitly detailing the CloudFront -> ALB -> ASG -> RDS data flow and Security Group boundaries. 2.2. Synthesizing Technical Contributions Structuring the Narrative: Organized the report logically, detailing the evolutionary journey from a Single Point of Failure (SPOF) architecture in Week 1 to a fully automated, Highly Available, and CDN-optimized environment by Week 10. Highlighting IaC & Automation: Emphasized the transition from manual provisioning (“Click-Ops”) to Infrastructure as Code (IaC) and CI/CD pipelines, showcasing an enterprise-level approach to cloud management. 2.3. Proofreading and Hugo Integration Markdown Formatting: Transcribed all weekly worklogs, technical challenges, and resolutions into standardized Markdown format (.md files) to be rendered by the Hugo framework. Technical Proofreading: Conducted a rigorous review of AWS terminology (ensuring correct usage of terms like “Availability Zones,” “Target Groups,” “Origin Access Control”) and verified that all CLI commands and JSON IAM policies included in the report were syntactically correct. UI/UX Review: Built and served the Hugo site locally (hugo server) to test navigation, hyperlink integrity, and the readability of code snippets and images on different screen sizes before the final deployment. 3. Key Takeaways & Challenges Takeaway: Technical documentation is just as critical as the engineering work itself. The ability to translate complex cloud architectures into a clear, readable report is a vital skill for aligning with stakeholders and mentors. Challenge: The architecture evolved so rapidly between Week 4 and Week 9 that the early drafts of the report contradicted the final system state. Resolution: I leveraged the Git commit history from the IaC repository established in Week 9. By reviewing the code changes (Pull Requests), I was able to accurately trace the architectural evolution and update the report’s timeline without missing any critical technical details.

Submitting Final Internship Report to Mentor for Review and Approval[cite: 3] 1. Weekly Objectives: Project Closure & Evaluation The final week of the Workforce Bootcamp marks the culmination of the 3-month cloud journey.
